lead: Both readings are about where we put what we have. Paul asks the Corinthians to give generously to the poor of Jerusalem, because “God loves a cheerful giver” and will never let the generous be the poorer for it. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus tells us to store up treasure in heaven, “for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” In the Apostles' Fast, fasting and almsgiving go together. The key words are sowing, cheerful and treasure.

set: Chapters 8 and 9 of 2 Corinthians are about the collection that Paul was gathering among his Gentile churches for the poor Christians of Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–27; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4). At the meeting in Jerusalem, James, Cephas and John had asked him to “remember the poor”, which, he says, “was actually what I was eager to do” (Galatians 2:10). For Paul the collection was more than relief. It was a sign that Jews and Gentiles were one Church. Some scholars think chapter 9 was first a separate note, perhaps to the churches of Achaia around Corinth; others read the two chapters as one appeal.
str: v. 6: the principle: sparing sowing, sparing harvest; generous sowing, generous harvest.
v. 7: give from the heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion.
vv. 8–9: God can give every grace in abundance, as the psalm says of the righteous.
vv. 10–11: the one who gives seed will multiply it, and the gift will become thanksgiving to God.
kw: The word that gives English “hilarious”, but here it means glad and willing. Verse 7 echoes the Greek text of Proverbs 22:8, which adds: “God blesses a cheerful and generous man.”
Having what one needs. The philosophers used it for being content with little. Paul uses it for having enough so that one can share abundantly.
In verse 6, “bountifully” is literally “with blessings”. A gift is a blessing to the one who receives it, and it calls down blessing on the one who gives.
vv: the one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.

Every farmer knows this. The seed thrown into the ground seems lost, but it is the only way to a harvest. Paul does not promise a financial return; the harvest he speaks of is the “harvest of your righteousness” (9:10).
Each of you must give as you have made up your mind, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
Paul will not force the Corinthians, though he has urged them strongly. A gift taken by pressure is not a gift. God looks at the heart of the giver more than at the size of the gift (Mark 12:41–44).
He scatters abroad, he gives to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.
From Psalm 112:9, which describes the righteous person who fears the Lord. Generosity to the poor is part of what Scripture calls righteousness.
You will be enriched in every way for your great generosity, which will produce thanksgiving to God through us;
The gift does not end with the poor who receive it. It turns into prayer: those who are helped give thanks to God. Almsgiving becomes worship.
ch: The Catechism recalls that from the very beginning Christians brought to the Eucharist, together with the bread and wine, gifts to share with those in need, and that this custom of the collection is inspired by the example of Christ, who became poor to make us rich (CCC 1351; 2 Corinthians 8:9). It also teaches that giving alms to the poor is a witness to fraternal charity and a work of justice pleasing to God (CCC 2462). In the Syriac tradition, as in the whole Church, fasting has always gone with almsgiving: what we deny ourselves is given to those who have less.

set: In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus has just spoken of almsgiving, prayer and fasting, done in secret for the Father who sees in secret (6:1–18). Now he turns to possessions. Our three verses begin a short section that goes on with the eye as the lamp of the body (6:22–23) and the saying that no one can serve two masters, God and wealth (6:24). The thought was familiar to devout Jews: Sirach had said, “Lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High” (Sirach 29:11), and Tobit taught that almsgiving lays up a good treasure (Tobit 4:9).
str: v. 19: do not store up treasures on earth, where they are lost.
v. 20: store up treasures in heaven, where they are safe.
v. 21: the reason: the heart follows the treasure.
kw: To heap up, to hoard. The noun is thēsauros, treasure or storehouse. Jesus does not condemn work or saving for one's family. He warns against making wealth the goal of life.
In the ancient world wealth was often kept in fine clothes, which moths eat, and in grain or metal, which decay. Brōsis means literally “eating”, anything that consumes.
In the Bible the heart is not only the feelings. It is the centre of the person, where we think, decide and love.
vv: where moth and rust consume and where thieves break in and steal;
“Break in” is literally “dig through”: houses were often built of mud brick, and a thief could dig through the wall. No earthly treasure is safe.
but store up for yourselves treasures in heaven,

Treasure in heaven is laid up by what we give and do for God and for others, above all for the poor. Jesus says to the rich young man: “sell your possessions, and give the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven” (19:21).
For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
Jesus does not say “where your heart is, there your treasure will be”, but the other way round. What we give our time and money to slowly shapes what we love.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse in teaching on the tenth commandment and the poverty of heart that Jesus asks of all his disciples (CCC 2544, 2551). Detachment from riches is necessary for entering the kingdom of heaven. St Augustine, preaching on this verse, calls the poor the porters who carry our goods ahead of us into heaven (Sermons, in substance). During the Apostles' Fast the Church invites us to look at our purse as well as our plate.

study: Paul says, “God loves a cheerful giver.” Do I give to God and to the poor gladly, grudgingly, or only when I am pressed?
If someone looked at how I spend my time and money, where would they say my treasure is?
